Goldman says hedge funds pile into shorts, with ETF shorts posting a 19-point weekly jump
body: Low hedge fund positioning cuts both ways. It limits the pool of forced sellers if the selloff resumes, but it also means a stabilization in prices could trigger short covering and re-risking that lifts stocks faster than fundamentals alone would suggest. The steady $150 billion of retail and retirement inflows provides a floor under large-cap indices, especially the mega-cap names those funds hold most. Homebuilders and other consumer-cyclical stocks with crowded shorts could be the most volatile if sentiment turns. With US markets closed for Thanksgiving, any re-risking is unlikely to show up until next week.
Professional investors are hedged and waiting for prices to stabilize, while retirement savers keep buying, and that split could shape how the next rally unfolds.

Hedge funds have moved from cutting risk to actively betting against the market, according to Goldman Sachs, a sign of how fragile sentiment has become during this month's selloff in technology stocks.

Vincent Lin, co-head of Prime Insights and Analytics in Goldman's FICC and Equities business, said on the bank's The Markets podcast that hedge fund clients reduced their exposure for five straight weeks. Last week the selling stopped, but clients turned more defensive by adding short positions in individual stocks and in index futures and ETFs. ETF short positions rose by about 19 percentage points in a single week, the third-largest weekly increase in the past decade. The episode was recorded on November 23, before Wednesday's US inflation data.

The rotation has favored defensive sectors. Consumer staples, utilities and real estate investment trusts have clearly outperformed over the past month, helped by lower volatility, less reliance on consumer spending and little connection to the AI trade. Within technology, clients have preferred the biggest cloud and AI platform companies, known as hyperscalers, for their stronger balance sheets and steadier earnings. On the short side, they have targeted economically sensitive consumer areas, especially housing and homebuilders, where positioning has fallen to multi-year lows.

Lin drew a sharp contrast between types of investors. Hedge funds and trend-following funds are near the bottom of their historical positioning ranges, and retail day traders have pulled back. But slower-moving retirement and mutual fund investors remain heavily invested, with ETF and mutual fund products taking in about $150 billion over the past month even as markets fell.

That gap matters for the near-term outlook. Lin said that when uncertainty is high, buyers tend to wait for higher prices before stepping back in. Hedge fund managers want to see prices stabilize before adding risk, and with the year nearly over, many are focused on protecting gains rather than chasing a rally. His models point to more supportive flows if prices steady or start trending higher.

Lin pointed to two drivers. The first is performance. Fundamental long-short equity funds were up about 17% at midyear but only about 7% at the time of recording, which he characterized as a setback rather than a collapse. The second is the AI story itself. Lin said "the best of the AI infrastructure returns is probably behind us," and that the trade is shifting toward how companies make money from AI, a transition he noted has historically been the hardest phase of major technology cycles.

He remains constructive on parts of the market. Lin still favors the hyperscalers and argues they should be relative winners if computing capacity stays tight, adding that any slowdown in AI spending could free up cash for buybacks. He also prefers healthcare over consumer staples, citing more attractive valuations and earnings drivers less tied to AI.

Lin flagged late-season tech earnings, US payrolls next week and November inflation data in about three weeks as the key tests, along with whether the Federal Reserve's hawkish stance holds. Since the recording, hotter-than-expected core PCE inflation has kept a December hike firmly priced. That leaves the near-term backdrop little changed for cautious hedge funds.

news.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6655 – Reuters estimate
body: The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets.

China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours.

Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations.

Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.

In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

news.title: Projectile explodes near tanker 50 nautical miles off Dubai as Gulf shipping attacks mount
body: Incidents without damage rarely move oil much on their own, but where this one happened matters for pricing. An attack near the UAE coast, inside the Gulf, puts loading routes that had looked relatively safe back in the risk picture, which tends to show up first in war-risk insurance premiums and tanker freight rates rather than in headline crude prices. Asian refiners, the biggest buyers of Gulf crude, are the most exposed to any further disruption. With US markets shut for Thanksgiving and liquidity thin, a more serious incident could cause an exaggerated price move before the full market returns.
No one was hurt and nothing was damaged, but a blast near a tanker off Dubai shows that the threat to Gulf oil shipping is no longer confined to the Strait of Hormuz.

A tanker reported an explosion from an unknown projectile close to the vessel about 50 nautical miles west of Dubai late on Wednesday, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said. It's the latest in a run of attacks on shipping that has kept Gulf oil supply under pressure.

The incident happened at 2130 GMT on November 25 (1630 US Eastern). The ship's master reported that the crew were safe and accounted for, with no damage to the tanker and no environmental impact. UKMTO, which monitors commercial shipping in the region, advised vessels to transit with caution while authorities investigate. It didn't identify the tanker or say who fired the projectile.

The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel between Iran and Oman, normally carries a large share of the world's seaborne oil. Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, Tehran has tried to close the strait, and the United States has imposed a blockade on Iranian ports. The International Maritime Organization has confirmed more than 130 incidents involving commercial vessels in the Gulf, the strait and the Gulf of Oman since the war began.

November has been especially busy. Reported attacks in and around the strait have reached their highest level since the conflict began, according to maritime data cited by CNN, as Tehran tries to reassert control while oil prices fall. This week, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers hit naval mines and caught fire in the strait despite a US escort, and Iran's navy said another tanker struck a mine east of the strait on Wednesday. On Sunday, UKMTO reported a tanker involved in an incident with military forces in the Gulf of Oman.

Wednesday's incident stands out for its location. It took place inside the Gulf, well west of the strait and close to the UAE coast, echoing earlier November attacks on tankers off Qatar and Saudi Arabia. That suggests the risk is spread across Gulf shipping lanes rather than confined to the chokepoint itself.

Oil is still moving, but at reduced levels. Shipping data from Kpler put oil flows through Hormuz at about half of pre-war levels as of November 24, and shipments through the strait fell in the first half of November as attacks increased. US-escorted transits have helped keep some traffic moving. Iran has also reportedly allowed vessels linked to Iraq, Qatar, China and India to pass, which suggests it is managing who uses the strait rather than shutting it completely.

That partial recovery explains why prices have eased in recent weeks despite the violence. Brent crude was trading around $91 a barrel late on Wednesday, up more than 2% on the day, but still well below its wartime peak.

The risk for the oil market is that each new incident, especially further inside the Gulf, raises insurance and freight costs and could deter shipowners who have only recently returned. For now, the market appears to be treating attacks that cause no damage as background noise. A strike that disables a tanker or hits loading infrastructure near the UAE or Saudi coast would be a different matter, and would likely bring back the supply premium quickly.
